principle_name: The Four Levers Framework — Volume, Timing of Cash, Length of Commitment, Timing of the Deal
author: Todd Caponi
when_to_use: Whenever a prospect raises a pricing or commercial terms concern. This framework replaces all ad-hoc discount responses and gives every negotiation a transparent, logical structure that builds trust instead of eroding it.
when_not_to_use: Do not use the levers as a manipulation tool — they only work when the pricing model is genuinely based on these four elements. Do not introduce the framework for the first time at the negotiation table — it should be laid during the earliest pricing conversations.
principle: Every for-profit company in the world prices its products and services based on four things: (1) Volume — how much the customer buys; (2) Timing of Cash — how fast the customer pays; (3) Length of Commitment — how long the customer commits; (4) Timing of the Deal — predictability of when the deal closes. These four levers are the only legitimate basis for any concession. When a prospect asks for a discount, the response is not to argue value or play ping-pong — it is to go through the four levers one by one and pay the customer in the form of a discount only in exchange for movement on one of these four elements.
questions_to_ask: Which of these four levers is most flexible for you — can you commit to more volume, pay faster, commit longer, or help us predict the timing?
Is the investment concern a budget issue, a value issue, or a procurement threshold issue?
What would need to change in these four areas for the investment to make sense for you?
recommended_action: Share the four levers framework early — during the first pricing conversation, not just at the negotiation stage. When a discount request comes, use all four levers as the agenda: go through each one, explain what MOTM is willing to pay for in the form of a concession, and let the prospect choose which lever to pull. Never give a concession without receiving something on one of the four levers.
what_not_to_do: Do not respond to a discount request by defending the ROI of MOTM — this approach has already failed if the prospect is in negotiation. Do not play ping-pong — counter-offering discounts without a framework signals that the original price was not real. Do not give concessions for free — every concession must be paid for in the form of a lever movement.
motm_application: When an MD asks for a discount on the MOTM retainer, the response is: Our pricing is based on four things — the scope of the engagement (Volume), payment timing (Timing of Cash), the length of the commitment (Length of Commitment), and when we get started (Timing of the Deal). Let me go through each one and see where we can find you a better price. This immediately changes the conversation from a price battle to a collaborative commercial discussion.

principle_name: Lever 1 — Volume: Pay the Customer for Committing to More
author: Todd Caponi
when_to_use: When a prospect is asking for a lower price and has the potential to commit to a larger or expanded scope of engagement than currently proposed — or when there is a second phase or additional service that could be added now in exchange for better pricing.
when_not_to_use: Do not use Volume as an excuse to upsell beyond what the prospect actually needs. The additional commitment must be genuinely valuable to the prospect — not a way to inflate the deal.
principle: The primary driver of any pricing model is Volume — how much the customer commits to. Larger commitments cost less per unit. Smaller commitments cost more. In the MOTM context, Volume represents the scope of the engagement — the number of SEs deployed, the markets covered, or the range of services included. When a prospect wants a lower price, the first question is whether they can commit to a larger scope now. If they can, MOTM pays for that in the form of a lower per-unit price. If they cannot, note it and move to the next lever.
questions_to_ask: Is there additional scope — more markets, more SEs, additional services — that you have been considering for later that could be included now?
If we commit to a larger initial scope, are there budget sources we could combine to make that work?
Is there a second phase of this engagement that we could incorporate into the initial commitment in exchange for better per-unit pricing?
recommended_action: When discussing the Volume lever, explain how the current pricing is based on the committed scope and that a larger commitment would result in a lower per-unit price. Ask whether there is scope that is planned for later that could be brought forward. Do not push Volume beyond what the prospect genuinely needs — present it as an option and let them decide.
what_not_to_do: Do not skip the Volume lever just because the prospect says they cannot expand the scope — always present it and explain how it works, then move on if it is not applicable. Do not use Volume pressure to push a prospect into committing to more than they need — this damages trust and creates buyer's remorse.
motm_application: When an MD says the MOTM retainer is too high for the first year: One thing that drives our pricing is the scope of the engagement. The pricing you have now is based on one SE covering this territory. If you would like to add coverage for the new market you mentioned earlier, a larger initial commitment would result in a lower per-SE price across the whole engagement. Does that make sense to explore? If not, let me show you the other three ways we can adjust this.

principle_name: Lever 2 — Timing of Cash: Pay the Customer for Paying Faster
author: Todd Caponi
chapter: Chapter 3 — The Second Lever: Timing of Cash
when_to_use: When a prospect wants a lower price and has the ability to pay annually up front rather than quarterly or monthly, or to accelerate payment for out-years in a multi-year engagement.
when_not_to_use: Do not accept slower payment terms without adjusting another lever. Every request to pay more slowly must be met with a corresponding movement on another lever — not a free concession.
principle: Every for-profit company prefers to receive cash faster rather than slower. Payment terms are a real commercial variable that affects cash flow, planning, and organisational stability. When a customer agrees to pay faster — annually up front instead of quarterly, or all years up front instead of year by year — MOTM pays for that in the form of a discount. When a customer asks to pay more slowly, they are asking MOTM to give up something real — and that requires a corresponding concession on another lever.
questions_to_ask: Our current proposal is based on quarterly payments. If you are able to pay annually up front, that is something we are willing to pay for in the form of a discount. Does that work for your cash flow planning?
For a multi-year engagement, if you are willing to pay for Year 2 up front along with Year 1, we will adjust the pricing accordingly. Is that something your finance team could support?
What are your standard payment terms — and is there flexibility to accelerate if the discount is meaningful enough?
recommended_action: Always set the Timing of Cash lever in the proposal — state clearly what payment timing the pricing is based on. When a prospect asks for slower payment terms, immediately use the four levers framework and explain that slower payment requires an adjustment elsewhere. When a prospect can pay faster, offer a specific discount in exchange.
what_not_to_do: Do not allow payment terms to slip silently — prospects will ask to pay more slowly as a default, and without a framework, salespeople give in without receiving anything in return. Do not offer faster payment as a discount lever only when the prospect pushes back — state it proactively as part of the pricing explanation.
motm_application: When a MOTM prospect says the annual retainer is too high: Our pricing is based on quarterly payments. If you are able to pay the first year up front in a single payment, we are willing to pay you for that in the form of a 5% reduction in the annual retainer. Paying up front is genuinely valuable to our business — and we want to pass that value back to you. Does that work with your budget cycle?

principle_name: Lever 3 — Length of Commitment: Pay the Customer for Committing Longer
author: Todd Caponi
chapter: Chapter 4 — The Third Lever: Length of Commitment
when_to_use: When a prospect wants a lower price and has confidence in the MOTM engagement but is hesitant about a multi-year commitment due to perceived risk. Explaining what a longer commitment earns them can shift the conversation from price to risk — and addressing the risk directly is more effective than discounting.
when_not_to_use: Do not push for unrealistically long commitments that the prospect cannot genuinely make. The commitment must be realistic and genuinely valuable to the prospect — not a mechanism to lock them in.
principle: Longer commitments are more valuable to a service provider because they enable better resource planning, lower client acquisition cost, and more predictable revenue. When a customer commits for two years instead of one, or three instead of two, MOTM pays for that in the form of a lower annual price. A common structure is 5% per additional year of commitment. The Length of Commitment lever also governs responses to requests for short-term pilots or proof-of-concept arrangements — these represent a very short commitment and should be priced accordingly.
questions_to_ask: The pricing you have is based on a one-year commitment. If you are willing to commit for two years, we would pay you for that longer commitment in the form of a 5% reduction. Does a two-year arrangement make sense given your growth plans?
What is the primary concern about committing for longer — is it about confidence in the results, or about internal budget planning?
If we can address your concern about [specific risk], would a longer commitment be possible?
recommended_action: Always state the Length of Commitment on which the pricing is based. When a prospect asks for a lower price, present the multi-year commitment option as one of the four levers and explain specifically what it earns them. If the prospect is reluctant due to risk, address the risk directly — do not just offer a discount.
what_not_to_do: Do not use Length of Commitment as a trap — the prospect must genuinely want to commit longer, and MOTM must genuinely intend to deliver over that period. Do not skip this lever because it feels like a big ask — present it and let the prospect decide. Do not grant Termination for Convenience clauses without repricing the engagement to reflect the absence of commitment.
motm_application: When a MOTM prospect wants a lower annual retainer: The current pricing is based on a one-year commitment. If you are willing to commit to a two-year engagement, we will pay you for that in the form of a 5% reduction in the annual retainer. A two-year commitment also gives you the benefit of continuity — the same SE, the same relationships, the same pipeline momentum — without the disruption of re-engaging a BD partner mid-cycle. Does a two-year arrangement make sense for where your business is going?

principle_name: Lever 4 — Timing of the Deal: Pay the Customer for Mutual Forecast Alignment
author: Todd Caponi
chapter: Chapter 5 — The Fourth Lever: Timing of the Deal
when_to_use: When a prospect is genuinely ready to engage MOTM but has not yet committed to a specific start date, or when the prospect is asking for a better price and has the ability to commit to a specific timeline that helps MOTM plan its resources.
when_not_to_use: Do not use fake expiring discounts or artificial deadlines — these destroy trust and train prospects to wait for end-of-quarter desperation discounts. The Timing of the Deal lever only works when the alignment is mutual and genuine.
principle: Every for-profit company benefits from predictability. Knowing when a new client engagement will start allows MOTM to plan its SE resources, onboarding capacity, and operational commitments. When a prospect is willing to mutually align around a specific start date and commit to it, that predictability is genuinely valuable — and MOTM pays for it in the form of a discount. This is fundamentally different from a fake expiring discount: the prospect chooses the date, it is mutual, and they have skin in the game. A prospect who helps MOTM forecast gets a better price. A prospect who cannot commit to a timeline does not — and does not feel pressured by an artificial deadline.
questions_to_ask: From the time we finalise the structure of this engagement, how long do you think it would take your organisation to sign and get started?
If you are willing to commit to starting by [date the prospect names], we are willing to pay you for that predictability in the form of a 5% discount. Does that work?
What steps remain internally before you could commit to a start date — and how long do those typically take?
recommended_action: Ask the prospect to name their own realistic start date — do not impose one. Once the date is named, build in a small buffer for unexpected delays. Offer a specific discount in exchange for mutual commitment to that date. If they commit and hit the date, honour the discount. If they miss the date, revisit the pricing — but do so transparently and without hostility.
what_not_to_do: Do not say if you sign this week I can give you 10% off — this signals that the original price was inflated and trains the prospect to wait. Do not use end-of-quarter dates as the artificial deadline — these are about the salesperson's targets, not the prospect's needs, and sophisticated buyers know it. Do not withdraw the discount punitively if the prospect misses the date — revisit it transparently.
motm_application: When a MOTM prospect agrees the engagement makes sense but has not committed to a start date: There is genuine value to us in knowing when we will be deploying our SE to your business — it affects our resource planning. If you are willing to help us with that by committing to a start date, we will pay you for that in the form of a 5% discount. What do you think is a realistic date to get started — and what steps do you need to take to get there? Once we agree on a date, we build it into the engagement terms.

principle_name: Set Pricing Expectations Early — Do Not Wait Until the Proposal to Discuss Investment
author: Todd Caponi
when_to_use: In the first or second meeting with any prospect. Pricing expectations should be set before the proposal — not revealed in the proposal for the first time. Sticker shock at the proposal stage is caused by concealing price during discovery.
when_not_to_use: Do not share a precise price before understanding the prospect's specific situation — share a range with clear qualifications about what drives the final number.
principle: Waiting to reveal price until the final proposal is one of the most common and damaging mistakes in professional services BD. When price is concealed until the end, the prospect's brain cannot properly evaluate the value against the investment — and when the number finally appears, sticker shock creates resistance that undoes months of relationship building. Sharing a pricing range early — along with an explanation of the four levers that determine it — builds trust, accelerates qualification, and makes the eventual negotiation easier. A prospect who knows the investment range from the first meeting can genuinely evaluate whether it makes sense for their situation.
questions_to_ask: Based on what we know so far, the typical MOTM engagement for a business like yours is in the range of ₹X to ₹Y per month. Is that range consistent with your expectations, or would it be helpful to discuss now rather than later?
If the investment is significantly different from what you were expecting, I would rather know that now so we can either adjust the approach or part ways before investing more of each other's time.
recommended_action: In the first or second meeting, share a pricing range based on the prospect's situation. State clearly that it is a range and explain briefly what drives the final number — scope, payment terms, commitment length. Ask whether the range is consistent with their expectations. If it is far off, address it immediately rather than proceeding to build a proposal they will reject on price.
what_not_to_do: Do not conceal price until the proposal — this is not strategic, it is a source of sticker shock and damaged trust. Do not share a precise price before understanding the situation — share a range. Do not assume the prospect will stretch their budget to meet your price — if they cannot, it is better to discover this in the first meeting than after a lengthy discovery process.
motm_application: In a first MOTM meeting with an MD: Based on what you have shared about your sales situation and the size of your business, a typical MOTM engagement for a company like yours runs between ₹X and ₹Y per month. That range is based on the scope of the engagement and the payment and commitment structure — both of which we can tailor. Is that range consistent with what you had in mind, or would it be helpful to discuss the investment expectations now rather than later? This single question saves weeks of wasted discovery.

principle_name: Never Discount Without Receiving Something in Return — Every Concession Must Be Paid For
author: Todd Caponi
when_to_use: Every time any concession is requested — whether on price, payment terms, contract length, or timing. No concession should ever be given for free.
when_not_to_use: This is a universal principle — it applies to every commercial negotiation without exception.
principle: Giving a concession without receiving something in return is paying the customer. If you charge ₹10 and give a 10% discount, you have given the customer ₹1 for nothing. Worse, you have told the customer that your price is not really your price — which triggers them to search for more easy discounts. Every concession MOTM gives must be paid for by the prospect in the form of movement on one of the four levers: more Volume, faster payment, longer commitment, or better timing. This is not about being rigid — it is about having a principled basis for every commercial decision that builds rather than erodes trust.
questions_to_ask: Before we look at adjusting the investment, let me walk you through the four levers that drive our pricing — that will show us where we have flexibility and what you would need to give us in return.
When you say you need the price to come down, can you help me understand what is driving that — is it a budget constraint, an approval threshold, or a value perception issue?
If we can find the right adjustment, what are you most flexible on — scope, payment timing, commitment length, or start date?
recommended_action: When any concession is requested, use the three-step response: (1) Be human — understand what is driving the request; (2) Review all four levers; (3) Discuss what movement on each lever the prospect can make in exchange for the concession. Do not propose which lever to pull for them — present all four and let them choose. The prospect who negotiates their own deal is far more committed to the outcome.
what_not_to_do: Do not offer a concession before going through the four levers. Do not tell the prospect you can give 10% off if they sign this week — this is a fake expiring discount that teaches them to wait and then ask for more. Do not accept the premise that your price needs to come down without first establishing what the prospect will give you in return.
motm_application: When a MOTM prospect says the retainer is too high: I hear you — let me make sure I understand what is driving that before we look at adjustments. [Listen.] Now, let me show you the four things that drive our pricing, and we can go through each one to see where we can find you a better number without MOTM absorbing the cost of the concession. [Walk through the four levers.] Which of these feels most flexible for your situation? This approach turns the discount conversation into a collaborative commercial discussion.

principle_name: Ditch the Fake Expiring Discount — Replace It With Genuine Timing Alignment
author: Todd Caponi
chapter: Chapter 5 — The Fourth Lever: Timing of the Deal
when_to_use: Whenever there is a temptation to create urgency through an artificial deadline or end-of-period discount. Replace the artificial deadline with a genuine timing conversation where the prospect chooses the date and earns a discount by committing to it.
when_not_to_use: Do not use this approach if the deadline is genuinely real and externally imposed — in that case, communicate it honestly and explain why. Genuine urgency is different from manufactured urgency.
principle: Fake expiring discounts — this price is only valid until Friday, end-of-quarter special, limited time offer — are one of the most trust-destroying tactics in B2B selling. They signal that the original price is not real. They train prospects to wait for desperation discounts. They make the prospect feel manipulated. And they actually cause prospects to delay, not accelerate — because a prospect who knows a discount is coming has no reason to act before the deadline. The replacement is genuine mutual alignment on timing: the prospect chooses a realistic date, commits to it, and earns a discount for the predictability that commitment creates.
questions_to_ask: From your perspective, what does the internal process look like from here to getting this signed — and how long does that typically take?
If we build in a couple of weeks of buffer for unexpected delays, what date would you feel comfortable committing to?
There is genuine value to us in knowing when this will start. If you can commit to that date, we will build a 5% discount into the engagement for that predictability.
recommended_action: When urgency is needed, ask the prospect to name their own realistic timeline — not the salesperson's quarter-end. Build in a buffer. Offer a specific discount for committing to that date. This creates urgency through the prospect's own self-interest rather than through artificial pressure.
what_not_to_do: Do not use phrases like this offer expires on or end-of-quarter pricing — these signal desperation and teach prospects to wait. Do not impose a date on the prospect — ask them to choose one. Do not withdraw the discount without a genuine conversation if the prospect misses the date.
motm_application: Instead of saying if you sign before the end of this month we can do better on the price, MOTM BD says: There is real value to us in being able to plan when our SE will start with your team. If you can commit to a start date and we can build that into the agreement, we will pay you for that in the form of a 5% discount. What date do you think is realistic for you to get this signed and get started? That question shifts the urgency from the salesperson's calendar to the prospect's own planning — and the resulting commitment is far more likely to hold.

principle_name: Termination for Convenience Represents No Commitment — Price It Accordingly
author: Todd Caponi
when_to_use: When a prospect requests a Termination for Convenience clause — the ability to exit the contract at any time for any reason. This is one of the most significant commercial concessions a service provider can make and must be priced accordingly.
when_not_to_use: Do not refuse Termination for Convenience outright with it's not our policy — this creates an adversarial position. Use the four levers framework to explain what the absence of commitment costs and let the prospect make an informed choice.
principle: Termination for Convenience means no commitment. When a prospect can exit at any time for any reason, the Length of Commitment lever reads zero. This is not a minor legal request — it fundamentally changes the commercial basis of the engagement. Pricing based on a one-year or multi-year commitment must be recalculated to reflect a month-to-month basis when Termination for Convenience is granted. This typically means a 30-35% price increase. Presenting this reality honestly — you can have it, but here is what it costs — is more effective and more trust-building than refusing it outright.
questions_to_ask: Can you help me understand why Termination for Convenience is important to you — is it a company policy, a flexibility need, or a confidence concern about the engagement?

You can absolutely have Termination for Convenience, but I want to make sure you understand what it means for the pricing — because our pricing is based on the Length of Commitment, and Termination for Convenience represents no commitment. Should I show you what the month-to-month pricing would look like?

Are there specific concerns about what might happen during the engagement that are driving this request — if so, those are things we can address directly through the warranty and Termination for Cause provisions that are already in the agreement.
recommended_action: When a prospect requests Termination for Convenience, go through the three-step response: (1) Be human — understand what is driving the request; (2) Review all four levers; (3) Explain that Termination for Convenience is available but represents a fundamental change to the Length of Commitment lever and will require repricing to month-to-month terms. Also point to the existing Termination for Cause and Warranty provisions as protections that address the underlying concern.
what_not_to_do: Do not say it is not our policy — this creates an adversarial position and signals inflexibility. Do not grant Termination for Convenience without repricing the engagement — this gives away the Length of Commitment lever for free. Do not ignore the impact on investor confidence and business planning that Termination for Convenience creates.
motm_application: When a MOTM prospect's legal team adds Termination for Convenience to the draft agreement: I understand why this clause is requested — and you can have it. But I want to make sure you understand what it means for the commercial terms. Our pricing is based on a committed engagement period. Termination for Convenience removes that commitment entirely, which means the pricing would need to reflect month-to-month terms — typically 30-35% higher. Alternatively, the Termination for Cause provisions already in the agreement protect you if MOTM fails to deliver as promised. Can we look at those together first, and then decide whether Termination for Convenience is still necessary?

principle_name: Transparency Begets Transparency — Cards-Faceup Negotiation Builds Trust at the Finish Line
author: Todd Caponi
when_to_use: As the foundational philosophy for all MOTM commercial conversations. Every negotiation is an opportunity to deepen trust — not to maximise extraction. The cards-faceup approach is the alternative to adversarial negotiation.
when_not_to_use: This philosophy does not mean revealing confidential business information or accepting any request without reciprocation — it means being honest about the basis for pricing and what drives commercial flexibility.
principle: Traditional negotiation theory assumes that each party starts with an inflated position and concedes toward the middle through a series of offers and counteroffers — which means both parties begin the negotiation by deliberately misrepresenting their actual position. This is antithetical to trust. In professional services, where the relationship must survive and grow long after the deal is signed, negotiating by deceiving each other at the goal line destroys the trust built during the entire BD process. The cards-faceup alternative: explain honestly what drives your pricing, what you are willing to pay for in the form of a concession, and why. Transparency begets transparency — when the seller lays their cards faceup, the buyer stops being adversarial and starts being collaborative.
questions_to_ask: I want to be transparent about what drives our pricing and where we have flexibility — is it helpful if I walk you through how we think about the commercial terms before we discuss specific adjustments?
What would make you feel confident that the pricing we arrive at is based on something sound — not just an arbitrary starting point to be negotiated down?
recommended_action: Before any negotiation conversation, frame the discussion as a cards-faceup commercial alignment — not a battle of positions. Share the four levers framework as the honest basis for the pricing. Explain what MOTM gets from each lever and what the prospect gets from moving it. This immediately changes the dynamic from adversarial to collaborative.
what_not_to_do: Do not use negotiation tactics designed to make the prospect feel they have won something they have not won. Do not start with an inflated price designed to be discounted down. Do not treat the negotiation as a zero-sum game — a prospect who feels they won by grinding MOTM down will not stay, refer, or expand.
motm_application: At the start of any MOTM commercial conversation: I want to be straight with you about how our pricing works and where we genuinely have flexibility — because I would rather build this engagement on a foundation where you understand exactly what you are paying for and why. Our pricing is based on four things: scope, payment timing, commitment length, and when we get started. Let me walk you through each one so we can find the right structure for your situation. This opening signals partnership rather than negotiation — and sophisticated buyers respond to it with remarkable openness.
